lessons.title: Briefing a case, and reading a judgment for what binds
lessons.summary: A brief is a discipline, not a summary: the facts that mattered, the question, the answer, the reason, and what the court did not decide.

sections.keypoint: A summary says what happened; a brief says what the case can be used for.
sections.h: A summary and a brief are different things

body.text: Two people read the same judgment about a burst pipe in a shoplot. One writes down what happened. The other writes down what the case can be used for.
The second is much shorter and much harder, and it is the only one worth writing. You are reading the judgment so that you can use it on facts that are not these facts.

Here is the test. Six months later, without the report in front of you, can your brief still tell you three things? The proposition, the facts it was reached on, and why the next case is or is not the same.
If your brief runs longer than a page, you have written a summary. That is not a matter of style. A brief that reproduces the judgment has not done the work of deciding what mattered.

sections.keypoint: Five things a brief must carry — and four of them are about the limits of the decision.
sections.h: The five things a brief must contain

items: **The facts that mattered.** The facts the decision turned on, and no others. A fact mattered if changing it might change the result. Lawyers call these the material facts, and picking them out is most of the work.
**Where the case was.** Which court, hearing what, on appeal from whom. A first ruling and a Federal Court ruling on the same words carry completely different weight.
**The question.** Written as a legal question, and narrow. Not 'was the defendant liable' but 'does an authority that takes on a repair job and then walks away owe a duty to the people living there'.
**The answer, with the reason.** The proposition, plus the step that gets from the facts to it. An answer with no reason attached is just a result, and results do not transfer.
**What was left open.** Points the court reserved, arguments nobody made, things it said it was not deciding. This is the part everyone skips, and the part that decides most later arguments.

body.text: Notice that four of the five are about scope. A case is authority for something narrower than its language suggests, and a brief that does not record the edge is a brief that will be stretched too far.

sections.keypoint: Read a judgment out of order: disposal first, then facts, then the reasoning.
sections.h: Read it out of order

body.text: Judgments are written for a reader who already knows the dispute, and you are not that reader. So read them in the order that gets you oriented fastest.
Start with the headnote for the shape of it. Then read the last few paragraphs, to see who won. Then the facts. Then the reasoning, from the beginning.

Never cite from a headnote. A headnote is the editor's summary at the top of a law report. It is not part of the judgment, and it is wrong often enough that citing it is a habit of being occasionally and confidently wrong.

Where several judges each write, work out which reasoning had a majority behind it before you rely on any of it. A powerful dissent — a judgment disagreeing with the result — is very quotable and binds nobody.

body.q: Five judges sit. Two of them write a powerful dissent that says exactly what your client needs. What is it worth?
options: It binds, because it is part of a Federal Court judgment
It can be quoted and argued from, and it binds nobody
Nothing, because a dissent cannot be cited
body.why: A dissent is a judgment disagreeing with the result. It is often the best-written thing in the report, and it lost. You may quote it, and a later court may find it persuasive. The trap is the first answer. What binds is the reasoning a majority stood behind, not everything printed under the court's name.

body.title: The order that gets you oriented fastest
body.caption: Read the headnote for shape, never for authority. It is the editor's summary, it is not part of the judgment, and it is wrong often enough to matter.
body.alt: Five steps, in this order. The headnote, for the shape of the case only — never cite it. The last few paragraphs, to see who won. Then the facts, which now mean something. Then the reasoning, from the issue forward. Then, where several judges wrote, find which reasoning had a majority before relying on any of it.

steps.label: Headnote
steps.note: the shape only — never cite it

steps.label: Find the majority
steps.note: before relying on any of it

sections.keypoint: Necessity makes a ratio, not length or eloquence — and a court's own description is evidence, not proof.
sections.h: Two things that mislead

body.text: Two things fool people about which part of a judgment binds. The first is size: it is natural to assume the long passage matters more than the short one.
A proposition is part of the ratio only if the result would change without it. Length, emphasis and eloquence are not evidence of ratio; necessity is.
body.source: Standard common law doctrine on ratio decidendi and obiter dictum

body.text: Put simply: ask whether the case would have come out the same way without that passage. If it would, the passage is commentary, however many pages it runs to.

A judge writes eleven paragraphs on whether public bodies should pay for their mistakes. He then rejects, in one sentence, the argument the appeal actually turned on. That sentence is the ratio. The eleven paragraphs are useful material for the next case and nothing more.

body.prompt: A Federal Court judgment says, in terms, that it is laying down a general rule. Before you read on — how much of that binds the next court?
options: All of it, because the court said what it was doing
Only as much as the decision actually needed
None of it, since a description is not a decision
body.reveal: What binds is what the decision needed. The court's own label is good evidence and it is not proof. Picking the first is entirely reasonable, and if anybody knows what a court is deciding it ought to be that court. It runs both ways in practice. Judges sometimes announce a general rule while deciding something narrow, and sometimes do the reverse.

body.text: The second trap is subtler. A court's own description of what it is deciding is evidence, not proof. Judges sometimes say they are laying down a general rule while deciding something narrow on the facts, and sometimes it goes the other way. What binds is what the decision needed.

body.title: The only test for ratio
body.caption: Length, emphasis and eloquence are not evidence of ratio. Necessity is. Eleven paragraphs of reflection can be obiter while one sentence carries the decision.
body.alt: A question — would the result change without this passage? — branching two ways. No: it is commentary, however long or eloquent it is. Yes: it is part of the ratio, because the decision needed it.
body.question: Would the result change without this passage?

sections.keypoint: Write the brief before reading anyone else's account, because you cannot un-read theirs.
sections.h: Write it by hand, and write it first

body.text: Write the brief before you read anyone else's account of the case. Once you have read a textbook's version of what a case decides, you cannot un-read it.
You will find that you agree with it — not because it is right, but because you no longer have a view of your own to hold against it.
This is the same principle as the problem questions here: produce first, check second. The other order feels more efficient and teaches almost nothing.

quiz.q: What makes a fact 'material' when you brief a case?
options: Changing it might change the result
It appears in the headnote
The judge mentioned it more than once
It was agreed between the parties
quiz.why: Materiality asks what would change the result, not what the judge stressed. If the outcome survives the change, the fact was background.
quiz.source: Standard case-briefing method

quiz.q: Why should you not cite from a headnote?
options: It is copyrighted separately
It only appears in paid reports
It never states the ratio
It is written by an editor and is not part of the judgment
quiz.why: The headnote is the editor's summary. It is useful for orientation and unusable as authority, and it is wrong often enough to matter.
quiz.source: Standard case-briefing method; see Williams, Learning the Law

quiz.q: A judgment gives eleven paragraphs to policy and one sentence to rejecting the argument the appeal turned on. Which is the ratio?
options: The eleven paragraphs
Both equally
Neither — the disposal is the ratio
The one sentence
quiz.why: Necessity, not length. The appeal failed because that argument was rejected, so that is what the decision rested on.
quiz.source: Standard common law method on ratio decidendi

quiz.q: Which part of a brief is left out most often, and decides most later arguments?
options: The names of counsel
The procedural history
What the court expressly did not decide
The date of the judgment
quiz.why: Points reserved and arguments never made mark the edge of the authority, and that edge is exactly what the next case fights about.
quiz.source: Standard case-briefing method

quiz.q: Why write the brief before reading someone else's account of the case?
options: Because textbooks are usually wrong
Because you cannot form an independent view after reading someone else's
Because it is faster
Because textbooks omit the facts
quiz.why: Produce first, check second. Reading the account first replaces your reading with theirs and leaves you nothing to compare.
quiz.source: Standard case-briefing method

lessons.title: Writing an answer under time, and where IRAC fails
lessons.summary: IRAC is scaffolding for the application, not a form to fill in. Most of the value is lost before the first sentence, in how the facts are read.

sections.keypoint: Most answers go wrong before the first sentence, in the reading of the task and the facts.
sections.h: Most answers go wrong in the first five minutes

body.text: Encik Zaid asks whether his employer can dock his pay for turning up late. You write a careful, accurate page about unfair dismissal. He was never dismissed.

body.prompt: You have just written an accurate page on unfair dismissal for a man who was never dismissed. Before you read on — where did that answer go wrong?
options: In the law, because the wrong rules were learned
In the first few minutes, in reading what was actually asked
In the writing, because the point was not put clearly enough
body.reveal: It went wrong before the first sentence. The law on the page can be flawless and it is still an answer to the question next door. Blaming the law is the natural response, because the law is the part that feels like the thing being tested. The fix is a slower first read, not a longer answer.

body.text: The commonest failure is not ignorance of the law. It is answering the question next door: advising the wrong person, missing a second issue tucked inside a clause, or writing well about a rule the facts never raised.
Read the task before the facts, then read the facts twice: once for the story, once with the task in mind, marking every fact that could carry legal weight.
body.source: Standard examination technique; the same discipline as identifying material facts in a case brief

body.text: Put simply: find out what you are being asked before you get interested in the story. Then go through the facts a second time, pencil in hand, marking anything that might matter legally.
A fact that looks oddly specific — a date, an amount, an exact form of words, who spoke first — is there because it does work. A specific you have not used is usually an issue you have missed.

sections.keypoint: IRAC makes your reasoning visible; it is scaffolding, not a form to be filled in.
sections.h: What IRAC is for, and what it is not

body.text: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. It is a way of making your reasoning visible to somebody else, and it is not a form to be filled in.
Its real value is that it forces you to state the rule before you use it. That is exactly the step people skip when they are not sure of it.

items: **Issue** — the legal question these facts raise, in one sentence, narrow enough to be answerable.
**Rule** — the provision or principle that governs it, and where it comes from. A section number and a case name, not 'the law says'.
**Application** — the rule against *these* facts, argued both ways where it is arguable. This is where the value is.
**Conclusion** — an answer to the question that was actually asked, taking a position.

body.text: The failure mode is a long Rule and a short Application: a page of accurate law, then two sentences of 'therefore X is liable'. That shows you can recall, not that you can reason, and the marking bands here are weighted against it on purpose.

body.q: An answer sets out the governing provision accurately for a page, then ends: 'therefore Rosli is liable'. What is missing?
options: The application
The issue
The conclusion
body.why: The rule is there in full, and so is a conclusion. What is missing is the step between them: which fact meets which part of the rule, and where the call is close. The third answer is the tempting one, because that ending does feel abrupt. A position is stated. It was simply never earned.

sections.keypoint: If your answer sees only one side you have probably missed something — argue both, then decide.
sections.h: Argue both ways, then decide

body.text: A question worth asking is genuinely arguable. If your answer sees only one side, either you have missed something or the question was easier than it looked, and the second is rare.

Aisyah posts a letter on Monday offering to sell her sewing machine for RM300. On Tuesday she posts a second letter taking the offer back, and it arrives on Wednesday. On Tuesday evening, before it arrives, Rosli posts his acceptance. Do not just assert the postal rule, which is the rule about when posting counts. Say what turns on whether taking an offer back works when it is posted or when it arrives, apply the rule, and then decide.
Then decide. An answer that lays both sides out and refuses to choose has done three-quarters of the work and thrown away the end of it.

sections.keypoint: Divide the time by the marks before you start writing, and hold to it.
sections.h: Time, and the arithmetic nobody does

body.text: Give each part of the work the share of time its weight deserves, and hold to it. Going ten minutes over on one part costs you more elsewhere than it can possibly earn where you are.
If you are studying for something formal, do the sum before you start writing. A forty-mark question in a two-hour paper is forty-eight minutes, and not a minute more.
This site times every problem attempt against a stated target for the same reason. The clock is not decoration, and a good answer at twice the length is not a good answer.

body.title: Minutes per question in a two-hour, hundred-mark paper
body.caption: Time divided in proportion to marks. Going ten minutes over on the big question costs more marks elsewhere than it can possibly earn where you are.
body.source: Arithmetic, not authority: minutes divided in proportion to marks for a two-hour, hundred-mark paper. Substitute the weighting of the paper you are actually sitting.
body.note: Do this arithmetic before writing the first sentence, and hold to it.

quiz.q: Where do answers to a set of facts most often go wrong?
options: In the conclusion
In citation formatting
In reading the facts and the task
In handwriting
quiz.why: Answering the question next door — wrong person advised, second issue missed — costs more than any gap in the law itself.
quiz.source: Standard examination technique

quiz.q: What is the characteristic failure of an IRAC answer?
options: Too many issues identified
Concluding too firmly
Citing the statute
A long Rule section and a thin Application
quiz.why: It shows recall rather than reasoning, and the marking bands are weighted to catch exactly that.

options: It is realism, and can be ignored
It is a distractor
It does legal work and you have not yet used it
It sets the jurisdiction

As long as it needs
About thirty minutes
About forty-eight minutes

options: Leave it open, since it is arguable
Take a position and say why
Set out a third view
Restate the rule

lessons.title: Civil and criminal: two systems, one set of facts
lessons.summary: The same act can be a crime and a civil wrong. Who sues, what must be proved, how sure the court must be, and what it can order all differ.

sections.keypoint: One event can produce a prosecution and a claim, running on separate tracks to different results.
sections.h: One event, two cases

body.text: A van driver in Shah Alam looks down at his phone and hits a motorcyclist. Two entirely separate things can now happen to him.
The State may prosecute him, and the motorcyclist may sue him. The two run on different tracks, and they can end differently without either being wrong.

Criminal proceedings are brought in the name of the State to punish; civil proceedings are brought by a private party to compensate or to obtain a remedy. The parties, the standard of proof and the available orders all differ.
body.source: Standard common law distinction; in Malaysia the prosecution power is vested in the Public Prosecutor by Art 145(3) of the Federal Constitution

body.text: Put simply: a prosecution asks the court to punish somebody, and a civil claim asks it to put somebody right. Different people bring them, different amounts of proof are needed, and the court can order different things at the end.

body.prompt: The van driver is prosecuted and acquitted. The motorcyclist then sues him on the same facts, with the same CCTV footage. Before you read on — can she still win?
options: No, because a court has looked at this and found it unproved
Only if she has evidence the prosecution never had
Yes, because her case has a lower bar to clear
body.reveal: She can win on the very same footage. An acquittal is not a finding that nothing happened. It is a finding that the case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. Her claim asks something easier: is it more likely than not? The first answer feels like fairness itself. Two courts asking different questions can honestly give different answers.

body.text: Being acquitted does not mean the thing did not happen. It means it was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. A civil court, on the same facts and a lower standard, may quite properly find that it did.

sections.keypoint: The gap between the two standards of proof does most of the work.
sections.h: How sure the court has to be

body.text: The difference in how much proof is needed does most of the work here.

items: **Criminal:** the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The burden stays with the prosecution, unless a statute expressly puts one on the accused.
**Civil:** the plaintiff — the person bringing the claim — must prove the case on a balance of probabilities, meaning more likely than not.

**Fraud alleged in a civil case:** this has been contested ground in Malaysia. The Federal Court has held that fraud in civil proceedings is proved on the balance of probabilities, not to the criminal standard.

body.text: So the same evidence can lose a prosecution and win a suit. That is not the system contradicting itself. It is the system working as designed, because what is at stake in the two cases is different, and so is the risk each is willing to run.

The prosecution cannot make the court sure enough that the van driver was the one holding the phone, so he is acquitted. In the civil claim the motorcyclist has only to show that it is more likely than not. The same CCTV footage can be enough there and not enough in the criminal court.

body.caption: The same event, two proceedings
rows: The Public Prosecutor, in the name of the State
To compensate, or to obtain a remedy
Liability or dismissal; damages or an injunction
body.source: Federal Constitution Art 145(3); standard common law distinction

body.q: A civil claim alleges fraud. How much proof does the person bringing it need?
options: Beyond reasonable doubt, because fraud is also a crime
On the balance of probabilities, as in any other civil claim
Somewhere between the two, as the judge thinks fit
body.why: The Federal Court has held that fraud alleged in civil proceedings is proved on the balance of probabilities. The first answer is the trap, and a natural one: a grave allegation feels as though it should demand more. The standard is set by the kind of proceeding, not by how serious the allegation sounds.

sections.keypoint: A prosecution belongs to the Public Prosecutor, not the victim, so forgiveness does not end it.
sections.h: Who owns the case

body.text: A prosecution does not belong to the victim. It belongs to the Public Prosecutor, the office that controls all criminal prosecutions and decides whether to start, continue or stop one.
That power comes from Article 145(3) of the Federal Constitution. The victim is a witness in the case, not a party to it, and cannot settle it.

A civil claim belongs to the person who brought it, who may settle it, drop it, or never bring it at all. That single difference explains most of what looks odd about each system from the other's side.
A complainant who forgives the accused can withdraw a civil suit. The same forgiveness does not end a prosecution, though in practice it may affect whether one is carried on.

sections.keypoint: Conviction, acquittal, plaintiff, liability — using the wrong system's word is noticed immediately.
sections.h: Different words for the same shape

body.text: The two systems use different words at every stage. Picking the wrong one is a small mistake that gets noticed immediately.

items: Criminal: the **prosecution** and the **accused**; a charge; a conviction or an acquittal; a sentence.
Civil: the **plaintiff** and the **defendant**; a statement of claim; a finding of liability, or a dismissal; a judgment, damages, an injunction.
Appeals in both go up the same ladder of courts, but by different statutory routes, and with different rules about when permission to appeal is needed.

body.text: Do not call a defendant 'guilty' of negligence, or say that a company was 'convicted' of breaking a contract. The slip tells a reader that the distinction has not landed, and it costs you before the substantive law is even reached.

quiz.q: The accused is acquitted of causing hurt. Can the victim still win a civil claim on the same facts?
options: No — the acquittal is conclusive
Yes — the civil standard is lower
Only if new evidence emerges
Only with the Public Prosecutor's consent
quiz.why: An acquittal means the case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. More likely than not is a different question.
quiz.source: Standard classification; the criminal and civil standards of proof differ

quiz.q: Who has the constitutional power to start or stop a criminal prosecution in Malaysia?
options: The complainant
The Public Prosecutor, under Art 145(3)
The trial judge
The Inspector-General of Police
quiz.why: Article 145(3) puts the prosecution power in the hands of the Attorney General as Public Prosecutor.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 145(3)

quiz.q: What is the civil standard of proof?
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
Clear and convincing evidence
Prima facie case
Balance of probabilities
quiz.why: More likely than not. The criminal standard is kept for criminal cases.
quiz.source: Standard classification; the civil standard is the balance of probabilities

quiz.q: Which phrasing is wrong?
options: 'The accused was acquitted'
'The defendant was convicted of negligence'
'The defendant was found liable in negligence'
'The plaintiff was awarded damages'
quiz.why: Conviction belongs to criminal cases. A defendant in negligence is found liable, not convicted.
quiz.source: Standard classification

quiz.q: A victim forgives the accused and asks for the matter to be dropped. What follows?
options: Both automatically end
The civil claim can be withdrawn; the prosecution is not the victim's to withdraw
Neither can be discontinued
The court must discontinue both
quiz.why: The suit belongs to the plaintiff. The prosecution is not the victim's to withdraw.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 145(3)

lessons.title: Reading a citation, and what a report tells you before you read it
lessons.summary: A citation encodes court, year, series and status. Read it properly and you know how much weight a case can carry before you read a word of it.

sections.keypoint: A citation is an address, and it also tells you how much the case weighs.
sections.h: What a citation is made of

body.text: You are handed a case name with a string of numbers after it. That string is an address, and it also tells you how much the case is worth.
Take *Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San & Ors* [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC). Every part of it does a job: the parties, the year, the volume, the series, the first page, and the court.

items: **Square brackets** round the year mean you need the year to find the volume. [2010] 2 MLJ 1 is volume 2 of the 2010 Malayan Law Journal. Round brackets would mean the volume number alone finds it.
**MLJ** is the Malayan Law Journal, **CLJ** the Current Law Journal, and **AMR** the All Malaysia Reports. The same case can appear in more than one of them, at different pages.

**The court**, in brackets at the end — (FC) for Federal Court, (CA) for Court of Appeal, (HC) for High Court. This is the most important part, and the part most often dropped when a citation is copied.

body.text: A citation with no court in it is a citation you cannot weigh. Find out which court decided it before you use it, because a High Court decision and a Federal Court decision on the same point are not interchangeable.

body.caption: A citation with no court in it is a citation you cannot weigh. A High Court decision and a Federal Court decision are not the same thing, and the string tells you which you are holding.
rows: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San & Ors
The name you cite it by
Square brackets mean you need the year to find the volume
Which volume of that year's series
Malayan Law Journal. CLJ and AMR are the others
Federal Court. Without this you cannot weigh the case

sections.keypoint: Unreported judgments are citable, but they have not been through any editorial check.
sections.h: Judgments that were never reported

body.text: Many judgments appear on the courts' own portal before, or instead of, appearing in a report series. These carry a case number rather than a report reference.
They can still be cited. But a judgment that has not been reported has not been through an editor either, so it is a little more likely to contain a slip.
Where a case exists in both forms, cite the report. Where it exists only as a court-issued judgment, say so, and give the case number in full so that a reader can find the same document.

body.prompt: You have a full citation: the parties, the year, the volume, the series, the page and the court. Before you read on — what does it tell you about whether the case is still good law?
options: That it was good law when the volume was printed
That nothing has overruled it, or the series would say
Nothing
body.reveal: Nothing at all. A citation is an address. It tells you where the judgment lives, and which court gave it, and not one word about what happened to it afterwards. The third answer is the assumption almost everybody makes without noticing they have made it. It is why a decision can be cited with confidence for years after it stopped being good law.

sections.keypoint: A citation says where a judgment was published and nothing about whether it is still good law.
sections.h: What a citation cannot tell you

body.text: A citation is an address. Knowing where a judgment lives tells you nothing about whether it is still good law.
A citation records where a judgment was published. It says nothing about whether the case is still good law.
body.source: Standard research practice; the absence of a free Malaysian citator is a limitation of the sources, not of the method

body.text: Put simply: the numbers tell you where to find the case, and nothing about whether a later court has since torn it up.
This is the hard limit of free research in Malaysia. The AGC portal and CommonLII will give you the text, but they will not tell you that the decision was overruled four years later.

That check needs a citator, the tool that tracks what later courts did with a case. In practice that means a paid one — CLJ, LexisNexis CaseBase, or Westlaw — or a systematic search for later cases citing it.

*Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit* was, for nine years, a Federal Court decision that anyone could find and cite. Its subject was indefeasibility of title: whether a registered owner's title can be attacked. It was also wrong, and the Federal Court departed from it in *Tan Ying Hong*. Nothing in the text of the first judgment tells you any of that.

sections.keypoint: Record which version of a statute you read and when — consolidated texts change quietly.
sections.h: Statutes are cited differently, and change more quietly

body.text: A statute is cited by its short title and, where useful, its Act number: the Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), or the National Land Code (Act 828, Revised 2020).
What matters more is which version you read. Amendments are not always obvious in a consolidated text, and every reprint carries a date.

Always record the version you looked at and where you got it. 'Section 26 of the Contracts Act 1950' is not a complete note; 'section 26, as printed in the AGC consolidated text retrieved on *date*' is.

quiz.q: In [2010] 2 MLJ 1, what do the square brackets round the year mean?
options: The case is unreported
The year is needed to locate the volume
The judgment was delivered in 2010
The report is a second edition
quiz.why: Square brackets mean the year is part of the address. Round brackets would mean the volume number alone finds it.
quiz.source: Standard Malaysian citation practice (MLJ, CLJ, AMR series)

quiz.q: Which part of a citation is lost most often when it is copied, and matters most?
options: The page number
The court identifier
The volume number
The party names
quiz.why: Without knowing whether it is (FC), (CA) or (HC) you cannot weigh the authority at all.
quiz.source: Standard Malaysian citation practice

quiz.q: What can a citation never tell you?
options: Which court decided it
Whether the case is still good law
Where the judgment is published
The year of the report volume
quiz.why: A citation is an address, not a status check. That is what a citator is for, and there is no free Malaysian one.
quiz.source: Standard research practice; free Malaysian sources include no citator

quiz.q: A case appears both on the courts' portal and in the MLJ. Which should you cite?
options: The portal version
Either, without comment
Both, always
The MLJ report
quiz.why: Cite the report where one exists. The unreported text has not been through editorial checking.
quiz.source: Standard Malaysian citation practice

quiz.q: What makes a note of a statutory provision complete?
options: The section number alone
The Act number alone
The section and the marginal note
The section, plus which version you read and when
quiz.why: Consolidated texts change quietly. The version you read, and the date you read it, are part of the record.
quiz.source: Standard research practice; consolidated texts are amended between reprints

for reading a report at the speed a case actually needs, rather than front to back

lessons.title: Analogy, distinguishing, and the honest use of precedent
lessons.summary: Distinguishing is an argument about which facts mattered, not a way of dodging an awkward case. Doing it badly is the most visible weakness in a legal answer.

sections.keypoint: Distinguishing is a claim about materiality, not a way of escaping a case you dislike.
sections.h: Almost no case is exactly like yours

body.text: You find a case that looks like yours. It is not identical, because nothing ever is. Does it help you, or does the other side get to use it?
The work is arguing that the differences do not matter, or that they do. Both arguments have the same shape: both are claims about which facts the earlier decision actually turned on.
Showing that a binding case turned on a fact your case lacks has a name. Lawyers call it distinguishing.

body.prompt: The binding case was about a rented shophouse and yours is about a rented flat. Nothing in the earlier reasoning turns on the kind of building. Before you read on — have you distinguished it?
options: No, because the difference has to be one the earlier reasoning leaned on
Yes, because the facts are plainly different
Only if the other side cannot find a closer case
body.reveal: Pointing at a difference is not distinguishing. Every case differs from every other in a hundred ways. If any difference would do, no decision would ever bind anybody. The first answer is the honest first instinct, and it is what weak answers do at length. The difference has to be one the earlier court's reasoning actually leaned on.

body.text: To distinguish a binding case, identify a material difference between its facts and yours — a difference such that the reasoning of the earlier decision does not reach your facts. A difference that the earlier reasoning does not depend on is not a distinction.
body.source: Standard common law method; follows from the definition of ratio decidendi

body.text: Put simply: it is not enough that the two cases differ. The difference has to be one the earlier court's reasoning actually leaned on.

'The earlier case was about a lorry and ours is about a van' is not a distinction, unless something in the reasoning turned on the size of the vehicle. Pointing at a difference is not distinguishing. You have to show that the difference does work.

sections.keypoint: Three moves in descending order of legitimacy, and a student answer is almost always making the first.
sections.h: Three moves, strongest first

items: **Distinguish.** The rule of the earlier case, stated properly, does not stretch to these facts. Legitimate, and open to any court.
**Confine it to its facts.** The earlier decision is read as narrowly as its result allows. Legitimate but weaker, and a court doing it is usually signalling that it is uncomfortable.
**Depart from it, or overrule it.** Open only to a court with the power to do it. The Federal Court may depart from its own earlier decisions, but does so sparingly and with reasons.

body.text: Almost always the move you want is the first. Saying that a Federal Court decision is simply wrong is not an argument a High Court can make. Writing as though it were shows that the hierarchy has not landed.

body.title: Three moves, in descending order of legitimacy
body.caption: A student answer should almost always be doing the first. Asserting that a Federal Court decision is wrong is not an argument available to the High Court.
body.alt: Three moves, most available first. Distinguish: available to any court, and a claim about materiality. Confine the case to its facts: legitimate but weaker, and usually a signal of discomfort. Depart from it or overrule it: only a court with the power, and sparingly.

layers.label: Distinguish
layers.note: available to any court; a claim about materiality

layers.label: Confine to its facts
layers.note: legitimate but weaker — usually a signal of discomfort

layers.label: Depart or overrule
layers.note: only a court with the power, and sparingly

sections.keypoint: Foreign decisions persuade rather than bind, and weigh least where a Malaysian statute occupies the field.
sections.h: Persuasive authority, and how to weigh it

body.text: Decisions of courts in other common law countries do not bind a Malaysian court. They are persuasive authority: a court may follow them but need not.
Their weight depends on three things. How similar the statutory scheme is, how senior the court was, and how well the reasoning fits conditions here.

The trap in Malaysian law is the codified subject, where Parliament has written the rules into an Act. Contract here is governed by the Contracts Act 1950, not by the English common law of contract. An English case helps only where the Act's words raise the same question. An English authority cited against the words of a Malaysian section is worse than no authority at all.

sections.keypoint: Set the earlier facts beside yours and say what differs and why it matters — three sentences beat a paragraph.
sections.h: Write it so a reader can check you

body.text: Set out the earlier case's material facts. State its rule in your own words. Put your facts beside it, and say what differs and why the difference matters.
Three sentences done properly beat a paragraph of assertion.

*The authority in the drainage case had taken on the job of maintenance and then abandoned it, and the loss was physical damage to goods. Here the authority never started the work, and the loss is lost trade. The first difference goes to whether a duty arose at all. The second was a point the earlier court expressly left open. That case does not decide ours.*
That is what the application band of a marking rubric is looking for. It is also why an answer that recites two cases and asserts a conclusion scores far lower than it feels like it should.

quiz.q: What makes a difference between two cases a genuine distinction?
options: The facts are not identical
The parties are different
The earlier case is older
The earlier reasoning depends on the fact that differs
quiz.why: Distinguishing is a claim about what mattered. If the earlier reasoning did not turn on it, pointing at it proves nothing.
quiz.source: Standard common law method on distinguishing

quiz.q: A High Court judge thinks a Federal Court decision is wrong. What is the legitimate move?
options: Distinguish it if the facts allow, and otherwise follow it
Decline to follow it
Overrule it
Treat it as persuasive only
quiz.why: The hierarchy binds. Departing from Federal Court authority is not a move open to the High Court.
quiz.source: Standard common law doctrine of stare decisis

quiz.q: Why are English contract cases used with particular care in Malaysia?
options: English cases are never persuasive
Contract is codified in the Contracts Act 1950
The English courts use a different standard of proof
Contract law is a state matter
quiz.why: The starting point is the words of the Act. An English authority helps only where the Act raises the same question.
quiz.source: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136); contract is codified

quiz.q: Which is the weakest of the three legitimate ways of handling an awkward precedent?
options: Distinguishing it
Confining it to its facts
Following it
Applying it by analogy
quiz.why: It is legitimate, but it usually signals discomfort rather than a reasoned limit.
quiz.source: Standard common law method on precedent

quiz.q: What does the application band of a rubric reward?
options: Putting the rule against these facts and showing what turns on the difference
Accurate recitation of the earlier cases
Naming the correct section
A firm conclusion
quiz.why: Reciting is the rule band. Application is the work of moving from the rule to the facts in front of you.
quiz.source: The rubric bands used by the problem questions in this app

reading.where: the chapters on precedent and on legal reasoning

lessons.source: Standard common law method on precedent, distinguishing and persuasive authority; the codification point follows from the Contracts Act 1950 occupying the field.
lessons.verify: Check the current practice of the Federal Court on departing from its own previous decisions before asserting anything about how freely it may do so — the position has been stated in several judgments and is not identical in all of them.
lessons.plateCaption: Dividers stepping between two cases. Distinguishing is a measurement of whether the earlier reasoning reaches these facts.

lessons.title: Aids to interpretation, and the presumptions a reader brings
lessons.summary: Section 17A directs a purposive construction. Around it sit the linguistic canons, the aids inside and outside the Act, and the presumptions a court starts with.

sections.keypoint: Section 17A directs a purposive reading, but only among meanings the words can actually bear.
sections.h: Start with what the Act tells the court to do

body.text: An Act says a licence may be refused 'in the public interest'. A council reads that widely; the stallholder reads it narrowly. Both readings fit the words. Which one wins?

body.prompt: The council reads 'in the public interest' widely, the stallholder reads it narrowly, and the words can carry both. Before you read on — how does a Malaysian court choose?
options: It takes the narrower reading, since it is the stallholder's licence at stake
It takes the reading that serves what the Act was passed to do
It takes whichever reading the ordinary dictionary meaning supports
body.reveal: Purpose decides, and a statute says so. The third answer is worth sitting with, because a dictionary feels like the neutral tiebreaker. All it can give you is the range of meanings a word will carry. Choosing between them is the actual work, and Malaysian law directs how the choice is made.

body.text: Malaysian law answers that with a statute of its own. Where the words can carry more than one meaning, the reading that serves what the Act was for is preferred.
In interpreting a provision of an Act, a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act is to be preferred to a construction that would not.
body.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

body.text: Put simply: that is s 17A of the Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, and it is known as the purposive approach. Of the readings the words can bear, take the one that advances what the Act was trying to do.

It is not a licence to rewrite. Purpose chooses between readings the words can carry; it does not authorise a reading the language cannot support. Where the words have only one meaning, purpose does not displace it.
Leaping to purpose without first showing that the words are capable of two readings skips the step that makes s 17A apply at all.

sections.keypoint: Look inside the Act first: long title, definitions, provisos, schedules — and marginal notes, which are not enacted.
sections.h: Aids inside the Act

body.text: Before looking anywhere else, look at the rest of the Act. Several parts of it are evidence of what the words mean.

items: **The long title and the preamble** — evidence of what the Act is for, and a court may use them as such.
**The interpretation section** — where the Act defines its own words. A definition there displaces the ordinary meaning for that Act, and it is the first place to look.
**Marginal notes and headings** — the heading printed beside a section, and a guide to how the drafter arranged things. They are not enacted text and cannot control a clear provision.
**Provisos, illustrations and schedules** — a proviso is a qualification attached to the provision it sits under, and is read with it, never as a rule standing on its own.

body.text: Read the whole section before you read the words you came for. The commonest interpretation mistake is quoting a sub-section that a later sub-section cuts down.

body.caption: Which aids are enacted, and which are not
rows: Evidence of purpose; cannot cut down clear words
Displaces ordinary meaning for that Act — look here first
Qualifies the provision it sits under; read with it
Operative, unless the Act says otherwise
Indicate arrangement; cannot control a clear provision
body.source: Standard canons of construction; Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967

sections.keypoint: Ejusdem generis and its cousins are aids, not rules, and they yield to the Act's evident purpose.
sections.h: Rules about language

body.text: Suppose a by-law bans 'cats, dogs and other animals' from a food court. Does 'other animals' include a cow?

Probably not. General words at the end of a list of specific ones are read as staying in the same family, and here the family is household pets. That habit of reading has a Latin name, and so do two others worth knowing.

items: **Ejusdem generis** — 'of the same kind'. General words after a list of specifics are read as limited to the same class as the specifics.
**Noscitur a sociis** — 'known by its companions'. A word takes its colour from the words around it.
**Expressio unius est exclusio alterius** — expressing one thing implies the exclusion of others. The weakest of the three, and easily overstated: a drafter's silence is often just silence.

body.text: These are aids, not rules. A canon that produces a result against the evident purpose of the Act does not win. Section 17A does.

body.q: A by-law bans 'lorries, vans, buses and other vehicles' from a lane. Does it stop a bicycle?
options: Yes, because a bicycle is a vehicle in ordinary speech
Yes, unless the council can show it meant something narrower
Probably not, because the general words stay in the family the list sets
body.why: This is ejusdem generis. The three named vehicles are all motor vehicles, so 'other vehicles' is read as confined to that class. The first answer is the trap: the word on its own is wide enough, and the company it keeps narrows it. Remember that this is an aid and not a rule. A clear purpose pointing the other way would beat it.

sections.keypoint: Courts start with presumptions — against retrospectivity, for mens rea, against ouster — each displaceable by clear words.
sections.h: What a court assumes before it starts

body.text: A court comes to a statute with a set of starting assumptions, called presumptions. Each can be displaced by clear enough words, and most hard arguments are about whether it has been.

items: That an Act does not operate backwards, particularly where it affects rights people already have, or creates a criminal liability.
That a criminal offence needs a guilty mind, unless the statute displaces that expressly or by necessary implication.
That Parliament does not mean to shut the courts out. A provision that tries to is an ouster clause, and it is read narrowly.
That Parliament does not mean to legislate against the Constitution, so where two readings are open the constitutional one is preferred.

body.text: Naming a presumption and then asking whether the statute has displaced it is a complete piece of reasoning. Naming it and stopping is not.

sections.keypoint: A dictionary gives the range of ordinary meaning, never the meaning in this Act.
sections.h: Aids outside the Act

body.text: A dictionary establishes the range of ordinary meanings a word has. It does not establish the meaning in this Act.
Earlier statutes on the same subject are legitimate context, and so is the mischief — the problem the Act was passed to fix.

Parliamentary material is a harder case. *Pepper v Hart* [1993] AC 593 is the House of Lords decision that opened the English door to it. It is used with more caution in this jurisdiction than that case might lead you to expect.

Do not build an argument on Hansard without checking the current Malaysian position on whether it may be used. Hansard is the official record of parliamentary debates, and confident answers on this point are frequently wrong.

quiz.q: What does s 17A of the Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 direct?
options: Prefer the literal meaning always
Read penal provisions narrowly
Prefer the construction favouring the subject
Prefer a construction that promotes the Act's purpose
quiz.why: Section 17A is the statutory purposive direction, but it chooses only between readings the words can bear.
quiz.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

quiz.q: When does the purposive approach become relevant?
options: Immediately, before reading the words
Only in criminal cases
Once the words are capable of more than one reading
Only where there is a preamble
quiz.why: Purpose chooses between available readings. Where the language admits only one meaning, there is nothing to choose.
quiz.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

quiz.q: 'Rifles, shotguns, pistols and other weapons' — which canon limits 'other weapons'?
options: Ejusdem generis
Expressio unius
Noscitur a sociis
The golden rule
quiz.why: General words following a list of specifics are read as confined to the same class.
quiz.source: Standard canon of construction; ejusdem generis

quiz.q: Which presumption applies to an ouster clause?
options: It is read narrowly, against ousting the court's jurisdiction
It is read broadly, to give effect to purpose
It is void
It is presumed retrospective
quiz.why: Courts start from a presumption against being shut out, and require clear words before they accept it.
quiz.source: Standard common law presumption against ousting the court's jurisdiction

quiz.q: What weight does a marginal note carry?
options: Enacted text of equal weight
Inadmissible for any purpose
An indication of arrangement that cannot control a clear provision
Conclusive of purpose
quiz.why: Marginal notes are not enacted words. They orient the reader; they do not decide the meaning.
quiz.source: Standard canon of construction; marginal notes are not enacted words

quiz.q: What should you check before arguing from Hansard in Malaysia?
options: The date of the debate
Whether it was in English
Whether the Act has a preamble
The current position on its admissibility
quiz.why: The English Pepper v Hart line does not transfer automatically, and confident answers on this are often wrong.
quiz.source: Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593 (HL); the Malaysian position on parliamentary material must be checked separately

lessons.title: The literal rule, and the absurdity it cannot survive
lessons.summary: The literal rule tells a court to give words their ordinary meaning. It still matters after section 17A, but it yields once a plain reading defeats the very purpose it was meant to serve.

sections.keypoint: Farhan the volunteer firefighter shows why a court starts with what the words plainly say.
sections.h: Give the words their ordinary meaning

body.text: Farhan volunteers with the fire brigade near a forest reserve outside Kuantan.
A by-law reads: any person found in the reserve carrying an implement capable of felling a tree commits an offence.
The by-law was written to stop illegal logging inside the reserve.
Farhan enters the reserve during a fire, carrying an axe to cut a firebreak.

body.prompt: Read the by-law literally. Does it catch Farhan, who is fighting the fire, not causing it?
options: Yes, an axe is an implement capable of felling a tree
No, because he is a firefighter
It depends on whether he actually damages a tree
body.reveal: Yes. The words are broad enough to catch him, and that is exactly the problem with reading them only literally.

body.text: A court gives statutory words their ordinary and natural meaning, unless the Act defines them differently.
body.source: Standard canon of construction, not itself a numbered provision

sections.keypoint: Absurdity is not mere unfairness. It is a result that fights the reason the provision exists.
sections.h: When the plain words defeat their own purpose

body.text: A reading is absurd when it defeats the very problem the provision was written to solve.
Farhan is trying to protect the reserve, not strip it for timber.
The by-law was aimed at illegal logging, and Farhan is doing the opposite of that.
In interpreting a provision of an Act, a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act is to be preferred to a construction that would not.
body.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

body.text: Section 17A gives a court the tool to prefer a narrower reading here.
Do not skip straight to purpose. First show the plain words can bear a narrower meaning too.

body.q: Why is Farhan's case a good example of an absurd literal result?
options: Because the literal reading catches conduct opposite to the mischief the by-law targets
Because firefighting is always lawful
Because the by-law does not define implement
body.why: The by-law was aimed at illegal logging. Catching a firefighter protecting the reserve fights its own purpose.

sections.keypoint: An unwelcome result is not the same as an absurd one, and courts do not conflate them.
sections.h: Absurd is a high bar

body.text: Absurd does not mean unwelcome, harsh, or bad for your client.
It means a result no reasonable Parliament could have intended, given what the Act was for.
A strict filing deadline may feel harsh to someone who misses it by one day. That is not absurdity. Parliament can rationally want a hard deadline.
Calling every unfavourable outcome absurd weakens the argument. Save the word for a result that truly contradicts the Act's own purpose.

sections.keypoint: Read the plain words first, then test them against the purpose before reaching for section 17A.
sections.h: What to do with a hard section

items: Read the words for their ordinary, grammatical meaning first.
Ask what problem the provision exists to solve.
Test whether the plain reading defeats that problem.
If it does, use section 17A to prefer the reading that does not.

body.text: Farhan's case resolves in his favour on this method.
The plain words catch him, but that reading fights the purpose behind the by-law.
Section 17A lets a court prefer the reading that lets him do his job.

lessons.source: Standard canons of construction (the literal rule and the absurdity qualification); Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A. The Farhan scenario is an invented illustration, not the facts of any reported case.
lessons.verify: Read section 17A in a current reprint of the Interpretation Acts before quoting it. The forest reserve by-law is invented for teaching and is not a real provision.

reading.where: section 17A, for how far purpose can push against a plain reading

lessons.title: The mischief rule, and the question it forces you to ask
lessons.summary: The mischief rule asks what defect in the old law an Act was passed to fix. It is the closest ancestor of Malaysia's purposive approach under section 17A.

sections.keypoint: Encik Zulkifli's landlord slips a note under his door, and the mischief rule decides if that counts.
sections.h: The old law, and its gap

body.text: Encik Zulkifli rents a small flat in Ipoh.
Before a recent amendment, a landlord could repossess a flat without any warning at all.
Tenants sometimes came home to find their belongings already on the street.
Parliament then added a rule: a landlord must give a tenant fourteen days' notice before repossessing the premises.

body.prompt: The landlord pushes a notice under Zulkifli's door while he is away at work for a week. Does that notice satisfy the rule?
options: Yes, a written notice was left as required
Yes, because the method of delivery does not matter at all
No, not if he had no real chance of seeing it in time
body.reveal: Not necessarily. The mischief was tenants blindsided by sudden eviction, and a hidden note can defeat that just as much as no notice.

sections.keypoint: This method is centuries-old English doctrine, named here without a citation, for reasons this lesson explains.
sections.h: Heydon's Case, and the four old questions

body.text: The mischief rule has a long history in English law.
It comes from a sixteenth-century case called Heydon's Case.
This lesson does not give Heydon's Case a citation. It is old English doctrine, not a Malaysian authority, and no Malaysian citation for it is verified here.

items: What was the law before this Act?
What problem, or mischief, did that earlier law fail to cure?
What remedy has Parliament now provided?
What is the true reason for that remedy?

body.text: Answer all four, and you have found the purpose the Act was written to serve.

sections.keypoint: The mischief rule finds a purpose. Section 17A tells a Malaysian court to prefer it.
sections.h: Where this method feeds into section 17A

body.text: The mischief rule is not a rival to section 17A.
It is a method for doing exactly what section 17A demands: finding the purpose behind an Act.
In interpreting a provision of an Act, a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act is to be preferred to a construction that would not.
body.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

body.text: Ask Heydon's four questions, then let section 17A choose the reading that answers them.

sections.keypoint: Mischief cannot invent a purpose the words themselves are unable to carry, however good the reasoning.
sections.h: The limits of asking about mischief

body.text: The mischief rule cannot rewrite words that will not bear the reading you want.
If the words only support one meaning, no amount of purpose talk changes that meaning.

body.q: Does the note under Zulkifli's door satisfy the fourteen-day rule?
options: Yes, because a written notice existed
Yes, because the statute only requires fourteen days to pass
No, because the purpose was to give him a real chance to prepare, and a hidden note defeats that
body.why: The mischief was surprise eviction. A notice nobody can reasonably see in time does not cure that mischief.

lessons.source: The mischief rule and Heydon's Case reasoning are old English common law doctrine, taught here as method without a Malaysian citation. Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A, for the modern statutory link. The Zulkifli scenario is an invented illustration.
lessons.verify: Heydon's Case is centuries-old English doctrine and is deliberately given no citation here; check any Malaysian authority before naming one yourself. Read section 17A in a current reprint before quoting it.

reading.where: section 17A, for how the mischief inquiry feeds the purposive direction

lessons.title: What law applies when the law changes underneath you
lessons.summary: An amending Act rarely says nothing about the past. Check its own transitional words before assuming a new rule reaches back to an old event.

sections.keypoint: Cik Farah is charged under one fine, and Parliament raises it before she is convicted.
sections.h: A fine that changed mid-case

body.text: Cik Farah is charged in March with selling food without a licence.
At that time, the offence carries a fine of up to RM2,000.
In June, Parliament raises the maximum fine to RM10,000 for the same offence.
Farah is convicted in September, after the increase takes effect.

body.prompt: Which fine applies to Farah: the RM2,000 in force when she acted, or the RM10,000 in force when she is convicted?
options: The RM10,000 fine, since that is the law now in force
The RM2,000 fine, since that was the law when she committed the offence
Whichever fine the judge considers fairer on the facts
body.reveal: The RM2,000 fine applies. A change to a penalty is presumed to apply only going forward, not to conduct already finished.

sections.keypoint: Courts presume Parliament does not disturb a right or a punishment already fixed before the change.
sections.h: The presumption against reaching backward

body.text: A statute is presumed to look forward, not backward.
This presumption is strongest where a change would increase punishment or take away an existing right.
Parliament can still make a change reach backward, but it must say so clearly.
Silence is not enough. An amending Act that says nothing about the past is read as prospective only.
This is why the amending Act itself is the first thing to check, not a general textbook rule.

sections.keypoint: A change to how a case is heard usually applies at once, unlike a change to the rule itself.
sections.h: Procedure is treated differently from substance

body.text: Not every change to the law affects a substantive right.
A change to forms, timelines, or which court hears a matter is usually procedural.
Procedural changes commonly apply immediately, even to a case already under way.
An Act shortens the time to file an appeal from thirty days to fourteen. That change is procedural. It can apply to appeals not yet filed, even from older decisions.
A change dressed up as procedure can still be substantive if it removes a real right, not just a form.

body.q: An amending Act shortens the appeal period from thirty to fourteen days, with no transitional words. Does it apply to an appeal not yet filed?
options: Yes, since a purely procedural change usually applies immediately, even to matters already under way
No, because the case had already started under the old law
No, because procedural changes never apply to pending matters
body.why: A shorter appeal window is procedural, not a change to a substantive right. Procedural changes commonly take immediate effect.

sections.keypoint: Always look for the Act's own transitional or savings words before reaching for a general presumption.
sections.h: Checking an amending Act properly

items: Find the commencement date of the amending Act.
Search the amending Act for a transitional or savings provision of its own.
If there is none, apply the presumption against retrospective effect on rights and penalties.
Ask whether the specific change is substantive or merely procedural.

body.text: Farah's case follows this path exactly.
No transitional words rescue the higher fine, so the presumption applies and the RM2,000 fine stands.

lessons.source: Standard common law presumption against retrospective effect, and the substance-versus-procedure distinction; Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 generally. The Farah scenario is an invented illustration, not the facts of any reported case.
lessons.verify: Check the specific amending Act for its own transitional or savings provision before applying any general presumption discussed here. No numbered transitional provision is cited in this lesson because none has been verified for this module.

reading.where: for the general default rules a court falls back on when an amending Act is silent

lessons.title: Regulations only go as far as the Act allows
lessons.summary: Subsidiary legislation is made under a power the parent Act hands down. Anything it does beyond that power does not bind anyone.

sections.keypoint: Ah Kow's factory is fined under a rule the parent Act never actually authorised.
sections.h: A regulation that reaches too far

body.text: Ah Kow runs a small factory in Klang.
The parent Act lets the Minister make regulations about the safety of machinery.
A regulation is then issued setting minimum wages for factory workers.
Ah Kow is fined for paying below the new minimum.

body.prompt: The parent Act only mentions machinery safety. Can a regulation made under it validly set wages?
options: No, a regulation cannot go beyond the power the parent Act actually gives
Yes, regulations can cover anything a Minister thinks necessary
Yes, as long as the regulation is published properly
body.reveal: No, it cannot. A rule-making power about machinery safety does not stretch to wages, however useful the topic.

sections.keypoint: A delegated power only authorises what its parent Act actually says, and nothing wider.
sections.h: Why the parent Act always wins

body.text: Subsidiary legislation exists only because an Act allows someone to make it.
That permission is called an enabling or rule-making power.
A regulation, order, or by-law made outside that power binds nobody.
Subsidiary legislation is valid only to the extent that it is authorised by the Act under which it is made. Anything beyond that authority is of no effect.
body.source: Standard doctrine of delegated legislation; no specific numbered provision is cited for this general principle

body.text: Lawyers call an excess like this ultra vires, meaning beyond power.

sections.keypoint: The same purposive direction that governs an Act also shapes how its regulations are read.
sections.h: Reading a regulation purposively too

body.text: Section 17A is written for Acts, but the same thinking carries over.
In interpreting a provision of an Act, a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act is to be preferred to a construction that would not.
body.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

body.text: Ambiguous wording in a regulation is read to serve the purpose of the Act that authorised it.
A purposive reading of a regulation still cannot rescue a rule the parent Act never empowered anyone to make.

sections.keypoint: The wage rule falls outside the safety power, so it cannot be enforced against Ah Kow.
sections.h: What happens to Ah Kow

body.text: The wage regulation was never within the Minister's safety-only power.
It is ultra vires, and void to that extent.

body.q: Why can Ah Kow ignore the wage regulation?
options: Because it was made under a power about machinery safety, not wages
Because he did not know about it
Because factories are always exempt from wage rules
body.why: A regulation only binds within the power its parent Act actually grants. Wages sit outside a safety-only power.

lessons.source: Standard doctrine of delegated legislation (ultra vires subsidiary legislation); Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A, for the purposive link. The Ah Kow scenario is an invented illustration, not the facts of any reported case.
lessons.verify: Check the specific parent Act's rule-making power before concluding a regulation is ultra vires. Read section 17A in a current reprint before quoting it.

lessons.title: Policy arguments in judicial reasoning
lessons.summary: Sometimes the rules and the cases run out, and a judge must ask what a ruling would do to everyone in a similar position. Malaysian courts say so openly in a few places, such as the third limb of the Caparo test, and do it quietly in many more.

sections.keypoint: Yusof had no contract with the bank at all, yet the bank wants him to answer for its loss.
sections.h: A question the rules do not answer

body.text: Encik Yusof is a licensed valuer in Johor Bahru. A bank asks him to value a house before approving a loan.
He values the house at RM650,000. He was careless, and it is worth closer to RM400,000.
The borrower stops paying, the bank sells the house, and the shortfall is RM250,000.
The bank never hired Yusof. The borrower did. Nothing in his contract with the borrower answers whether he owes the bank anything at all.

Sometimes no existing rule or precedent decides a case squarely, and a court must reason its way to an answer instead of reading one off. A policy argument asks what a ruling would do to everyone in a similar position, not only to the parties in front of the court.
body.source: Standard jurisprudential material on judicial reasoning

sections.keypoint: Certainty, spreading risk, and protecting a class of claimant are typical policy reasons, not private opinion.
sections.h: What courts count as a policy reason

body.text: A policy reason is not a judge's personal opinion about fairness. It is a claim about what an entire class of case needs.

items: Certainty — will people be able to plan their affairs once this becomes the rule.
Spreading risk — can one side insure against the loss more cheaply than the other.
Protecting a class — does one side usually have less power to protect itself.
Floodgates — would a ruling for the bank let in many more claims like it.

body.text: In Caparo Industries plc v Dickman, a House of Lords case on auditor liability, the test for a duty of care has three parts.
Foreseeability, proximity between the parties, and whether imposing a duty would be fair, just, and reasonable.

The third limb of the Caparo test for a duty of care asks directly whether imposing a duty would be fair, just, and reasonable. That is a policy question stated in the open, not a technical rule with a fixed trigger.
body.source: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL)

sections.keypoint: An apex court states policy more openly than a court bound tightly by precedent below it.
sections.h: How openly a court says so

body.text: Not every court reasons this openly. A court low in the hierarchy is bound by precedent and has less room to invoke policy directly.
An apex court such as the Federal Court has more freedom, because it is not simply following someone else's answer.
A policy argument dressed up as if it were a rule is worse than an honest one. Say plainly that you are arguing about consequences, and defend the consequence you predict.

body.prompt: A new case asks whether a food delivery rider owes a duty of care to a pedestrian he nearly hits while speeding. Should the court's reasoning mention traffic on the roads generally?
options: No — only the two people in this case matter to the court's reasoning
Yes — a rule here will govern every rider and pedestrian in a similar position
Only if the rider's employer asks the court to consider it
body.reveal: Yes. A ruling here becomes a rule for every rider and every pedestrian afterward, so the court reasons about the class, not only these two people.

sections.keypoint: Name the class affected, name the value at stake, and say why it beats the other side's value.
sections.h: Using a policy argument yourself

body.text: A policy argument you make must do three things, or it is just an opinion wearing a wig.

items: Name the class of case affected, not only the two parties in front of the court.
Name the value at stake — certainty, protecting the weak, or spreading a cost fairly.
Say why that value should beat the value the other side is relying on.

body.text: For Yusof's bank: imposing a duty on valuers who know their reports will reach a lender protects lenders generally, at a cost valuers can insure against cheaply.

body.q: Why is 'imposing a duty would be fair, just, and reasonable' a policy question rather than a rule?
options: Because it has no fixed trigger and asks the court to weigh consequences
Because it appears in a House of Lords judgment
Because it only applies to auditors
body.why: A rule fixes its trigger in advance. This asks the court to weigh what imposing the duty would do, which is a policy judgment, not a checklist.

lessons.source: General jurisprudential material on policy reasoning in adjudication, illustrated with the third limb of the Caparo test for a duty of care.
lessons.verify: Nothing here states a rule of Malaysian law and none of it needs a citator beyond the Caparo citation itself. Check the current Malaysian formulation of the duty of care test before relying on Caparo directly.

lessons.title: Hypotheticals and the floodgates argument
lessons.summary: A floodgates argument predicts that a ruling will let in far more claims than the court can manage, and it can be right or wrong. The answer is never to deny more claims will follow — it is to show a boundary that keeps the class identifiable.

sections.keypoint: Farid's own contract was with the shopkeeper, yet he wants to sue the manufacturer directly.
sections.h: A claim that seems to open a door

body.text: Encik Farid buys a sealed bottle of soy sauce from a sundry shop in Ipoh.
He pours it over rice and finds a dead lizard near the bottom. He becomes ill for three days.
Farid wants to sue the manufacturer directly. His contract of sale was with the shopkeeper, not with the manufacturer at all.
The manufacturer's lawyer objects: allow this, and every buyer of every sealed product could sue every manufacturer directly, whatever went wrong.

A floodgates argument predicts that deciding a case one way will let in a flood of future claims the legal system cannot manage. It is an argument about consequences for the system, not about these two parties.
body.source: Standard jurisprudential material on judicial reasoning

sections.keypoint: A floodgates claim predicts how many future cases will follow, and predictions can be tested.
sections.h: What the argument actually claims

body.text: A floodgates argument is a prediction, not a fact. It says a ruling will cause many more claims of the same kind.
The prediction can be tested. Ask how many people are actually in Farid's position, and whether they have any other reason not to sue.
This is close to the objection raised against Mrs Donoghue's claim in 1932 — that a manufacturer should not answer to the whole world.
In Donoghue v Stevenson, part of the dissent warned that recognising a general duty like this had no obvious stopping point.
The answer to a floodgates argument is not to deny that more claims will follow. It is to show a limiting principle exists that keeps the class of claimants bounded and identifiable.
body.source: Standard common law reasoning on limiting principles in negligence, illustrated by Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (HL)

sections.keypoint: Donoghue answered the floodgates fear with a limit, not by denying more claims would follow.
sections.h: Answering it: find the limit, or accept the flood

body.text: The majority in Donoghue v Stevenson did not deny that more claims would follow. They answered with a limit instead: a duty runs only to someone who could not inspect the product before using it.
That limit — foreseeability and no chance to inspect — is what keeps the class of claimants bounded. It is not everyone who ever bought anything.
A floodgates argument used without naming any limiting principle is just an assertion dressed as prediction. Show the boundary, or the argument is only a fear.

body.prompt: A new claimant wants to sue a bridge's original builder fifty years after it opened, for a defect only now discovered. The builder warns of a flood of claims from every old structure in the country. Is that a strong floodgates argument?
options: No, because the class can be bounded by how many structures actually have this defect
Yes, because age alone shows the class of claimants cannot be bounded
No, because builders are never liable for old work
body.reveal: The second answer. The real question is how many structures share the actual defect, not how many structures exist in the country. That is a testable number, not a vague fear.

sections.keypoint: State a number and a boundary; without both, a floodgates claim is rhetoric rather than argument.
sections.h: Using the argument, and rebutting it

body.text: To use a floodgates argument well, name the boundary a ruling would need to cross. Say what class of case would be let in, and how large it is.

items: Identify the class of future claimants the ruling would affect, not just this one.
Estimate whether that class is actually large, or only feels large.
Show whether an existing limit — proximity, foreseeability, a time limit — already bounds it.

body.text: Against Farid's claim: the class is not everyone who buys anything, only buyers of a sealed product who could not have inspected it. That class is already bounded by the same test Donoghue set.

body.q: What actually defeats a floodgates argument?
options: Showing that a limiting principle already bounds the class of claimants
Proof that the courts have enough time to hear the new cases
Pointing out that the argument is unpopular with claimants
body.why: A floodgates fear is answered by a boundary, not by denying more claims exist. Foreseeability and proximity are the boundaries negligence actually uses.

lessons.source: Standard jurisprudential material on the floodgates argument in judicial reasoning, illustrated with Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (HL).
