lessons.title: Obiter dictum, and how much weight it carries
lessons.summary: Obiter dictum is anything a judgment says beyond what the case in front of the court actually needed. It can still carry real weight, especially from a senior court reasoning carefully, even though it does not bind.

sections.keypoint: The court only needs to answer one question here; anything beyond that is not needed to decide it.
sections.h: A remark that goes further than the case needs

body.text: Puan Nadia sells her interior design firm to Encik Boon for RM900,000, paid in two parts.
She agrees not to compete for two years, or forfeit the last RM200,000 owed to her.
She opens a rival studio after fourteen months. Boon refuses to pay the RM200,000, calling the clause a penalty the court will not enforce.
A court deciding this dispute only needs to answer one question: is this particular clause, on these facts, a penalty. Anything it says beyond that is not needed to decide the case.
A statement in a judgment that goes beyond what was necessary to decide the case before the court is obiter dictum. It does not bind a later court the way the ratio decidendi does.
body.source: Standard common law doctrine on obiter dictum

sections.keypoint: Obiter carries weight from the seniority of the court and the care the reasoning shows.
sections.h: Why obiter is not automatically worthless

body.text: Not binding does not mean unimportant. An apex court's careful, considered remark can shape the law even though no later court must follow it.
In Cavendish Square Holding BV v Talal El Makdessi, the United Kingdom Supreme Court went far beyond the two contracts before it.
Several justices set out, at length, how the whole doctrine on penalty clauses should be reframed for future cases.
Much of that discussion went beyond the minimum needed to decide whether these two specific clauses were penalties. Later courts have leaned on it anyway.

The weight of an obiter remark depends on the seniority of the court, how carefully it was reasoned, and how directly it addresses the point later courts must decide. A careless aside carries little; a considered discussion by an apex court carries much more, even though it does not bind.
body.source: Standard common law doctrine on obiter dictum, illustrated by Cavendish Square Holding BV v Talal El Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67

body.prompt: The Federal Court, in deciding a straightforward contract dispute, adds three paragraphs speculating about how the same reasoning might apply to leases generally. Is that obiter?
options: No, because the Federal Court's remarks always bind
Yes, and being from an apex court it may still carry real weight
Yes, and it therefore carries no weight at all
body.reveal: Yes. It goes beyond the lease dispute at hand, so it does not bind. Coming from the Federal Court and reasoned with care, it may still guide later courts strongly.

sections.keypoint: Calling a remark obiter says where it sits, not whether the court got it right.
sections.h: Obiter is not the same as wrong

body.text: Students sometimes treat 'obiter' as a way to dismiss a passage they find inconvenient. That is a mistake.
Calling something obiter tells you it does not bind. It tells you nothing about whether the reasoning inside it was any good.
Do not use 'merely obiter' as a substitute for an argument. Say why the remark is unpersuasive, or accept that a later court may well adopt it anyway.

body.q: A High Court judgment contains a considered discussion of a point not strictly needed to decide the case. What is the correct description?
options: It is obiter, and its weight depends on how carefully it was reasoned
It is the ratio, because the judge clearly believed it
It is void, because only the Court of Appeal may reason this way
body.why: A remark not needed to decide the case is obiter regardless of which court gave it. Its persuasive weight still depends on the reasoning and the court's seniority.

sections.keypoint: Ask what the court had to decide, then test whether a passage was needed to decide it.
sections.h: Finding the line yourself

body.text: To find the line, ask one question of any passage: was this needed to decide the case in front of the court?

items: If removing the passage would change the order the court made, it is probably ratio.
If removing it changes nothing about the order, it is obiter, however confident the tone.
If several judges reason differently to the same result, compare them before you claim a single ratio.

body.text: In Nadia's dispute, the finding that RM200,000 was a genuine penalty is the ratio. A passing view on how forfeiture clauses in employment contracts should be treated is obiter.

lessons.source: Standard common law doctrine on obiter dictum and ratio decidendi, illustrated with Cavendish Square Holding BV v Talal El Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67.

lessons.title: Reasoning from principle versus reasoning from a rule
lessons.summary: A rule fixes its trigger and applies once that trigger is met. A principle states the purpose behind the rule, and lets a court ask what that purpose requires on facts nobody wrote the rule for.

sections.keypoint: Halim broke the curfew rule by twenty minutes, but he was fighting a fire at the time.
sections.h: The same words, two ways to read them

body.text: Encik Halim runs a vegetable stall in a wet market in Kuantan. Market rules say stallholders must leave the premises by ten at night.
At 9:50pm, a fire breaks out in the wiring near the fish section.
Halim stays until 10:20pm, helping two elderly stallholders out and dousing the flames with a hose before the fire brigade arrives.
The market's management wants to end his licence. He broke the curfew rule, on its plain words, by twenty minutes.

A rule fixes a trigger and applies once that trigger is met, regardless of why. A principle states the purpose the rule serves, and a court reasoning from principle asks what that purpose requires on these facts.
body.source: Standard jurisprudential material on rules and principles in adjudication

sections.keypoint: A rule-based answer checks only whether the trigger was met, nothing about why.
sections.h: Reasoning from the rule

body.text: Reasoning from the rule is mechanical, in the best sense. Was the stallholder present after ten? Yes. The rule is broken.
This is predictable and cheap to apply, and it is why the rule was written as a fixed time rather than a vague standard.
On this reading, Halim's reasons for staying do not matter. The clock is the whole test.
A purely mechanical reading can produce an answer nobody who wrote the rule would have wanted. That is the cost of choosing predictability over judgment.

body.prompt: Halim's licence review committee reads the curfew rule literally: present after ten means breach, full stop. Before you read on — is that reasoning from a rule or from a principle?
options: From a principle, because it considers what the curfew was for
Neither — a committee cannot reason at all
From a rule, because it applies the trigger without asking why it exists
body.reveal: From a rule. The trigger — presence after ten — is checked and applied, with no question asked about what the curfew is actually protecting.

sections.keypoint: A principle asks what the rule is actually for, then measures conduct against that purpose.
sections.h: Reasoning from the principle behind it

body.text: The curfew rule exists to clear the market safely and keep it orderly overnight. That is the principle behind the words.
Reasoning from the principle asks a different question: did Halim's presence after ten defeat that purpose, or serve it?
Answered this way, staying to fight a fire and evacuate people is not the mischief the curfew was written to stop.
Courts reach for a principle like this most often when the existing rules run out — a genuinely new kind of case the rule-writer never had in mind.

Before 1932, English law protected buyers of dangerous products only through a set of narrow, specific categories. In Donoghue v Stevenson, the House of Lords instead reasoned from a general principle: do not injure your neighbour.
The neighbour principle in Donoghue v Stevenson answered a case the existing narrow categories did not clearly reach, by asking what the underlying purpose of the law of negligence required.
body.source: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (HL)

sections.keypoint: Principle answers a wider range of cases but is more contestable and less predictable than a rule.
sections.h: Living with the choice

body.text: Reasoning from a broad principle is powerful exactly where rules run out, and risky for the same reason.
A principle stated too widely decides cases nobody has thought through yet, with no earlier case to discipline the answer.
Caparo Industries plc v Dickman pulled back from Donoghue's wide principle, deciding new duty-of-care cases incrementally, by comparing them to established categories instead.
Two honest judges can disagree about a hard case for exactly this reason: one reasons from the rule's words, the other from what the rule is for.

body.q: Why did Caparo move away from Donoghue's broad neighbour principle toward an incremental, category-by-category approach?
options: Because the neighbour principle had been formally overruled by Parliament
Because auditors are outside the scope of the law of negligence
Because a broad principle can decide unforeseen cases with no earlier case to discipline the result
body.why: A wide principle is powerful precisely because it reaches new situations, and that is also why it is harder to predict and easier to contest.

lessons.source: General jurisprudential material on rules and principles in adjudication, illustrated with Donoghue v Stevenson and Caparo Industries plc v Dickman.
lessons.verify: Nothing here states a rule of Malaysian law beyond the two citations used as illustration. Check the current Malaysian formulation of the duty of care test before relying on either case directly.

lessons.title: Reading an Act, and knowing which version you are holding
lessons.summary: A downloaded Act can be years out of date, and nothing on the page warns you. Checking the version you are holding is a habit, not a one-off task.

sections.keypoint: An Act can be passed, gazetted, and still not yet apply to anyone.
sections.h: Two dates on the same Act

body.text: Wei Sern is a pupil in a Petaling Jaya firm. His supervisor asks whether a clause needs to be registered under the Contracts Act 1950.
He opens a PDF of the Act on his laptop. It is the copy he saved during his law degree, three years ago.
A statute has more than one date attached to it. The date Parliament passed it is not the same as the date it took effect.
An Act does not necessarily take effect on the day it is passed. Many Acts provide that they come into force on a date fixed later, by order or notification.

body.prompt: Wei Sern's PDF is three years old, and the section he needs has not visibly changed. Before you read on — what does that tell him?
options: Nothing, until he checks whether an amendment or commencement order has been made since
That the section is settled, since nothing in his copy looks different
That only sections people litigate over ever change, so a quiet section is safe
body.reveal: Nothing, until he checks. A three-year-old copy cannot show him an amendment made in year two. The Act he is holding may already be superseded, and it would look exactly the same on the page.

sections.keypoint: A reprint carries its own date, and that date is the only thing it actually guarantees.
sections.h: The reprint, and what it promises

body.text: The Attorney General's Chambers publishes a consolidated reprint of most Acts. A reprint folds every amendment into one clean text, up to a stated date.
That date sits in the reprint's front matter, easy to miss and easy to skip past.
A reprint is current only to the date printed on it. Anything amending the Act after that date will not appear, however new and official-looking the document is.
body.source: Attorney General's Chambers, Malaysia; standard practice for consolidated reprints

body.text: A clean, official-looking PDF is not proof of currency. Read the date on the front page before you read anything else.
An amendment passed after the reprint's date exists as its own separate Act. It has to be read alongside the reprint until the next one absorbs it.

sections.keypoint: A repealed section can sit in an old textbook or download looking exactly like law.
sections.h: A section that was quietly repealed

body.text: Repeal is the other trap. Parliament can delete a section, or the whole Act, and an old copy will not show the gap.

An Act on hire-purchase is repealed and replaced by a new one. A student still working from a five-year-old textbook will quote sections that no longer exist, and every word will look correct on the page.
A citation that once worked can stop working overnight. Check whether the Act itself, not just the section, is still the one in force.

sections.keypoint: Four checks turn a downloaded PDF back into a source you can actually rely on.
sections.h: What to check, every time

items: Find the date printed on the reprint itself, not the date you downloaded it.
Search for any Act that amends this one, passed after that date.
Check whether the provision you need has actually commenced, if the Act was ever silent on the date.
Write down the date you checked, next to the section you relied on.

body.q: A pupil finds a clean, official-looking reprint of an Act with no visible amendments marked. What should she still do before relying on it?
options: Check the reprint's own date, and search for anything amending it since
Trust it, since the Attorney General's Chambers only publishes current law
Ask a lawyer, since a pupil cannot make this judgement herself
body.why: A reprint is a snapshot, not a promise that nothing has changed since. Checking its date and searching for later amendments is the only way to know.

lessons.source: General practice on statutory currency; the Attorney General's Chambers portal for reprints and consolidated texts. The Contracts Act 1950 is named only as an illustration of a section a reader might be checking.
lessons.verify: This lesson names no specific commencement provision or amending Act on purpose. Confirm the current reprint date and any later amending Act at the Attorney General's Chambers portal before relying on any section, including one already familiar to you.

lessons.title: Finding a case when you do not have its name
lessons.summary: Most real questions start with no case name at all, only a subject. A subject search works differently from typing a name into a search bar, and it is worth doing properly.

sections.keypoint: Most real questions arrive as a subject with no case name attached at all.
sections.h: A subject, not a name

body.text: Azman's client says her employer changed her shift pattern without warning. She asks if that is allowed.
Nobody in the office remembers a case on it. There is no name to type into a search bar.
A search engine wants a name, or at least a distinctive phrase. A subject search works differently, and it starts somewhere else.

items: Name the legal category first: is this a contract question, an employment question, or both?
Find the Act likely to govern it, and read its own words before searching for cases.
Only then look for cases, and look for them by subject, not by guessing a name.

sections.keypoint: A digest lists cases under a subject heading, so you can trace how a point developed.
sections.h: A digest sorts cases by subject

body.text: A digest is a subject index: a list of cases sorted by legal topic rather than by name or date.
Under a heading such as variation of employment terms, the cases appear together, oldest first, whichever report volume each one sits in.
A digest organises cases by subject rather than by name or date of report. It is the tool for a question that starts with a topic and no case name.
body.source: Standard legal research practice

body.text: Free Malaysian sources rarely offer this. A subject digest is usually part of a paid research service, alongside a citator.
Without a paid digest, build your own. Search the free portal using the Act's own words for the concept, not your own paraphrase of it.

body.prompt: Azman searches a free judgment portal for 'unfair change of shift pattern' and finds nothing. Before you read on — what is the likely reason?
options: The point has never reached a Malaysian court
Free full-text search is unreliable, and his phrase may not match the Act's own words
Employment disputes are never reported in full
body.reveal: Full-text search on a free portal depends on matching words, not matching ideas. A judgment on this exact point may use the Act's own language, not Azman's phrase. Try the statutory term next, not a paraphrase of the question.

sections.keypoint: An annotated Act prints short notes of relevant cases under the section itself.
sections.h: Let the annotated Act do some of the work

body.text: Some published editions of an Act print a short case note under each section, naming decisions that considered it.
This is a shortcut, and a genuinely useful one. It points you straight at cases already sorted by section.
An annotation is written at a point in time, like a reprint. A case decided after it was printed will not be there, however recently you bought the book.

sections.keypoint: Search by the Act's own words and by the legal category, not by a guess at a name.
sections.h: Two words worth more than a name

body.text: Two searches beat one guess. Search the free portal using the Act's exact wording for the concept.
Then search a library catalogue or a textbook's index for the same subject, and follow its footnotes to the cases it names.

items: Search the statutory term itself, in the words the Act actually uses.
Search a textbook's subject index, and read the cases its footnotes point to.
Note which of these you tried and what each one returned, even when a search finds nothing.

body.q: Azman's search for his own phrase found nothing. What should he try before concluding there is no case on the point?
options: The Act's own statutory term, and a textbook's subject index
Give up, since a thorough search already failed
A different search engine, using the same phrase
body.why: A failed search on one phrase is not a failed search on the subject. The statutory term and a textbook's index are two more genuinely different routes in.

lessons.source: General research practice on subject search and case digests; the Attorney General's Chambers portal and free case-law portals for primary search.
lessons.verify: This lesson names no specific digest, database or product, and states no fact about any particular one, on purpose. Confirm what search tools you actually have access to before planning a search around any of them.

lessons.title: Secondary sources, and how much each is worth
lessons.summary: A textbook, a journal article, a firm's blog post and a forum comment are not the same kind of thing. This lesson is only about that third pile, and how much weight sits inside it.

sections.keypoint: Everything Nabila has open is commentary — useful, and none of it is the answer.
sections.h: Five tabs, and none of them is the law

body.text: Nabila is preparing written submissions for a tenancy tribunal. She has five tabs open: a textbook chapter, a journal article, a law firm's blog post, a forum thread, and a video.
None of these is the law itself. All five sit in the same pile: somebody talking about the law, rather than the law or a judgment.
That pile is not one thing. Some of it is worth citing, and some of it is worth nothing at all.

sections.keypoint: Named authorship, editorial checking, and a recent date separate a source worth citing from one that is not.
sections.h: What makes one more trustworthy than another

items: Who wrote it, and can they be named and checked? An unsigned post cannot be held to anything.
Did an editor or a publisher check it before it went out, or did it go straight online?
How recent is it, and does it say which edition or version of the law it describes?
Does the writer have something to sell? A firm's article markets the firm as much as it explains a rule.

body.caption: Five sources, roughly ranked
body.alt: Five kinds of secondary source, ranked by three questions. A textbook and a journal article are named, edited, and not selling anything. A firm's client alert is usually named, sometimes edited, and is selling the firm. A forum thread is rarely named and not edited. A short video is sometimes named, not edited, and often selling something.

body.text: A secondary source is worth more the more it can be checked: a named author, an editorial process behind it, and a stated date against the current law.
body.source: Standard practice in evaluating legal commentary

body.q: A law firm's blog post explains a rule clearly, with no author named anywhere on the page. What does the missing name tell you?
options: That it cannot be checked or held accountable, so weigh it carefully
Nothing, since firms only publish accurate material
That the post is automatically wrong
body.why: An unnamed writer cannot be checked, questioned, or held to what they wrote. That does not make the post wrong. It makes it worth less than a source you could actually check.

sections.keypoint: An excellent textbook from years ago can describe a section that has since changed.
sections.h: Even a good textbook can be out of date

body.text: A textbook's authority does not freeze time. Check its edition date against the date of any amendment you already know about.
A textbook chapter explains a section clearly and well, and has for years. If the section was amended after the book went to print, the explanation is now wrong, however well it reads.
Citing an old edition as though it were current is a common, avoidable mistake. Note the edition and its date whenever you rely on a textbook.

sections.keypoint: A good secondary source leads you to the primary law faster than it answers the question itself.
sections.h: Where a secondary source actually helps

body.text: The proper use of a textbook or article is as a map. It should point you to the Act, the section, and the leading cases.
Read those primary sources yourself once you are pointed at them. Do not stop at the map and call it the destination.

body.prompt: Nabila's textbook chapter cites a section and two cases clearly, with full references. Before you read on — has she finished her research?
options: Yes, a textbook this clear can be cited directly
No — she still has to read the section and the cases herself
Only if it is the newest edition she can find
body.reveal: No. A clear textbook has done her a favour by naming what to read next. It has not done the reading for her, and a court will want the primary source, not a description of it.

lessons.source: Standard practice in evaluating legal commentary. This lesson is only about secondary sources; the order of primary sources and the rules of precedent are covered elsewhere in this module and in the foundations material.
lessons.verify: This lesson names no specific textbook, journal, firm or website as an example of good or bad practice, on purpose. Judge any real source in front of you against the four questions here rather than against a label.

lessons.title: Keeping a trail someone else can follow
lessons.summary: A note that only makes sense to you is not a research trail. This lesson is about building one that a supervisor, a colleague, or you in a year, can actually check.

sections.keypoint: A private note and a trail meant for someone else are not the same document.
sections.h: A note that only makes sense to you

body.text: Farah spends a full day researching a question for her supervising partner. She finds the answer, and hands over one paragraph.
Her partner asks where it came from. Farah cannot remember which of six tabs gave her the point that mattered.
A private note only has to work for you, tomorrow. A trail has to work for somebody else, who was not in the room.

body.prompt: Farah's partner asks where her one-paragraph answer came from, and she cannot say. Before you read on — what went wrong?
options: Nothing — a correct answer needs no further explanation
She kept a private note in her head, not a trail someone else could check
She should simply have researched faster
body.reveal: She kept the kind of note that only works for her, and only today. A trail has to survive being handed to somebody who was not in the room.

sections.keypoint: Every step needs its source, its date, and what it actually returned, including nothing.
sections.h: What a checkable trail contains

items: The question, written down exactly as it was asked.
Each source you checked, in the order you checked it.
What each source actually said, or that it said nothing useful.
The date you checked it, since the answer can change after.

body.caption: A page from Farah's trail
rows: The general rule and its exceptions
body.alt: A three-row research log. Step one checked the Contracts Act 1950 section 26 and found the general rule and its exceptions. Step two searched a free case-law portal by keyword and found nothing on point. Step three checked a textbook chapter and found two named cases. All three are dated the tenth of September.

body.text: A research trail records the question, every source checked, what each one returned, and the date. A dead end is worth recording too, so nobody repeats it by accident.
body.source: Standard research practice

sections.keypoint: A search that found nothing is still worth writing down, so it is not repeated.
sections.h: Dead ends are part of the record

body.text: Farah's second search returned nothing. That is still a fact worth keeping, not a failure worth deleting.
Written down: 'Searched the free portal for X, 10 Sept, nothing found.' A colleague reading this a month later does not repeat the search. They do not waste the same hour.
A trail with only the sources that worked hides exactly how thorough the search was. Keep the ones that failed too.

sections.keypoint: A trail is finished when someone else could redo it and land in the same place.
sections.h: Handing it over

body.text: The test of a trail is simple. Could your supervisor retrace every step, using only what you wrote down?

body.q: Farah's trail states the answer she reached, but not the sources she checked to get there. What is missing?
options: The whole trail — a conclusion with no working behind it is not checkable
Nothing — the answer is what her partner actually needs
Only the dates, since the sources matter less than the answer
body.why: A conclusion with no record behind it can only be trusted, never checked. The entire point of a trail is that nobody has to trust it blindly.

body.text: Write the trail as you go, not from memory afterwards. Memory drops the dead ends first, and the dead ends are half the value.

lessons.verify: Confirm the wording of section 26 and its exceptions in a current reprint before relying on it for anything beyond this illustration of how to log a search.
